image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Scatter plot** with labeled points and a **diagonal reference line**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **No faceting or small multiples**
- **No stacking**
- Uses **direct labels** for countries
- Includes a **45-degree reference line** for comparison between x and y values

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Percentage of **40+ year-olds** who say the world is getting better | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Percentage of **15- to 24-year-olds** who say the world is getting better | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual point identity and direct text labels |
| Equality/reference between x and y values | Quantitative reference | Diagonal line (y = x) |

comments.raw_comment: I noticed a generational divide between youths and adults. When asked if the world is getting better with each generation, youth ages 15-24 seemed more optimistic than the 40+ especially within ‘first world' countries such as the US, UK, Japan and Germany. Only 3 of 20 countries have older generations who believe the world is improving which leads me to wonder if countries not mentioned believe it’s not improving at all. I wonder if people between ages 15-24 will have a different mindset as time goes on since the world keeps changing and what factors contribute to the populace’s perception on whether the world is becoming a better place. This relates to me and my community since I’m part of the youth and am surrounded by my age group at school but also have older cultured parents and family so I can see the different mindsets first hand between the youth and the older generation. I have noticed that older generations seem to make generalizations about the younger generations and that there is a common agreement among each side with many people between ages 15-24 finding themselves in line with each other about feeling the world being a better place as we progressively move forward with each generation. The Battle Between Generations: Where Is The World Headed?

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that in general, more younger people ages 15-24 think that the world is getting better with each generation rather than older people ages 40+ do. I find this really interesting because often people think of younger generations as being especially pessimistic and negative, whereas this graph says otherwise.  The US is one of the farthest points away from the line, with a positive residual, meaning that more young people think the world is getting better, and less older people do. I wonder if what the world was like as the older people were growing up shaped how they feel about future generations - they might be negative because newer ideas and concepts that they are not used to are surfacing, and many people do not like change.
I wonder what other countries' data looks like - is there a specific reason that they chose to only survey/include these countries? If they included other countries, this graph might look completely different. I also wonder about the ages in between - how do 25-39 year olds feel about the world?
This relates to me and my community because I am in the younger generation, and I'm surprised at how positive so many young people are, because it often feels like the opposite.

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, I see that significantly more amount of young people, 15-24-year-olds, believe the world is getting better with each generation.  Two countries that I immediately notice have large differences between the opinions of the younger and older groups surveyed are the United States and Japan. For the United States, almost 65% of the younger generation believes the world is getting better with each generation while about 35% of the 40+ group believes this. For Japan, about 60% of the 15-24-year-old group believes the world is getting better with each generation while about 25% of the older group believes the prompt. Both countries have such vast changes with the younger groups' beliefs compared to the older. I wonder why these specific two countries have the largest differences. I also wonder why Indonesia's percentages are so high up for both groups, having over 75% for both. This relates to me and my community because my country, the U.S is part of this poll taken and my age is also considered in the graph, so it's interesting to see how my own generations view our progress of bettering the world. A title appropriate for this graph would be "Each Generations' Thoughts on the Bettering of the World."

comments.raw_comment: In nearly all of the countries surveyed, more young people (aged 15-24) believed the world was getting better than middle aged to older people (ages 40 ). There were no significant outliers that had the opposite relationship. I also noticed that the differential between the two was greatest in countries that had relatively low population growth rates, like the United States and Japan. I learned in my human geography class that relationships like that can end out exacerbating issues for the older dependent population. I wonder if potentially that is one of the reasons why older people tend to have a more pessimistic viewpoint on where society is headed. I also wonder why some countries, like Indonesia, were so overwhelmingly positive in their views across the board, but some countries were overall very negative. I think it likely is influenced by the situation of internal affairs within that country. I’m not familiar with the political systems of each country here, but I think it’s also plausible for that to have a significant impact on people’s world views. This graph could be titled “Is the world improving with the new generation? They think so.”

comments.raw_comment:
15- to 24-year-olds tend to say the world is getting better with each generation. I notice that there doesn't seem to be too much correlation between which countries are more positive or negative towards the future. It seems there are some countries from around the world, but this graph does not include many others like China or Korea, or Norway just to name a few.

I wonder if the older generation is generally less positive towards the future because they have lived longer and seen what the past was like and the present and future as less good. For example, a 50-year-old who has probably lived their childhood and adolescence without phones and computers and the internet might be more opposed to it than a 15-year-old who has probably lived most of their life with phones and the internet. I also wonder if older generations are generally more pessimistic or if they are just pessimistic towards the future of the world. In addition, I wonder what would this graph look like if it were taken 20 years ago, or 50, or 100? 

This relates to me and my community because I have noticed that my friends who fall in the 15- to 24-year-olds category do seem to be more open to change and more readily positive towards the future. However, adults around me are more neutral or slightly negative towards what the future holds. 

"The World is Getting Better, But for Who?"

comments.raw_comment: I notice that many countries have a higher percentage of young people who are more optimistic about our world’s development, with elderly people showing less optimism. Especially in countries like the US, there is a huge difference, with about 70% of young people believing the world is getting better and only about 30% of the elderly believe it’s getting better. However there are some countries like Indonesia, India, and Nigeria who have relatively even numbers of people, young and old, who think that the world is getting better. I wonder why higher percentages of people in less developed countries say the world is getting better. Does it have anything to do with the fact that they see their own lack of development and then they see how the world around them has many improvements, and perceive improvements from around the world as much greater things than people from more developed countries might perceive them? This graph poses many questions about perspective, especially with the topic of improvement being very perspective based. This relates to my community because I am part of the younger generation, so it is very uplifting to see that large amounts of young people have very positive outlooks on the world. I would title this graph “Optimism: the new divide between generations”.

The first thing I noticed is how 'Young' people tend to lean towards the idea of "the world is getting better with each generation"  more than 'older' people. As in the graph, you can see that most of the 15 - 24-year-olds in the provided countries fall between the 50-75% range, with none under 25%. However, when looking at the Y-axis for people over the age of 40, most countries fall below 50%, and have a significant amount under 25%. 

There is not exactly a noticeable trend among the data, however you do notice that most of the '1st world' countries have a much higher 'optimistic' younger population than an older one. As you can see in the graph, the US, UK, Japan and Germany are all within the 50-75% range on the X-axis (younger people believing the world is getting better), meanwhile on the Y-axis (Older people believing that the world is getting better) all the previously mentioned countries fall below the 50% mark. 

There is an anomaly within this result, which would be Indonesia, as both the younger and older generations agree that the world is getting better as time goes on. This is likely due to the fact that Indonesia's economy has increased by over 600% since the year 2000, this would obviously see a great increase in the quality of life and general welfare of the populace. Under such conditions, it is quite understandable why Indonesia's population generally have such 'high hopes' for the future.

What do you notice

     In general, the young are more optimistic than the old, they think the world is getting better with each generation much more. There are very few countries listed that go below the dividing line (India, Nigeria, Morocco), and none that deviate far right and down from the dividing line. Indonesia has high percentages on both sides, while countries like Brazil and mail have low percentages.

What do you wonder

    I wonder what causes the younger generation to think more optimistically about the future. Why is Indonesia so high in both metrics but Brazil so low? Are countries that are currently in rapid development (like India) more likely to be higher on the scale?

How does this relate to you and your community

comments.raw_comment: I can see from this chart that young people in most countries believe that the world is on a good path. But except for three countries, young people in other countries will be more optimistic about the development of the world than the elderly. But according to a psychological survey by UC Davis, 51 is the peak of optimism, but it doesn't seem to show this in this chart. This raises my question: is this data reliable enough? What is the specific age of the person who answered this question? But when we assume that the data of this questionnaire is reliable, a very interesting question arises. Can an optimistic attitude towards the development of the world really show that this person is an optimistic person? Because in my opinion, this is a very objective problem. I am in China because the epidemic protection is very strict. In China, entering shopping malls or some public areas requires a QR code to prove that they are healthy, but many middle-aged and elderly people are rejected because they don't have mobile phones or can't use them. This will make them feel abandoned, abandoned by the world. This is just a small example, but when we re-examine this chart, I believe everyone will have the answer.

comments.raw_comment:
The first thing I notice is the clear lean in the graph that favors towards most countries having a higher percentage of 15-24-year-olds who are optimistic about the future of our world. I also notice that Morocco, Nigeria, and India are the only countries where this is not true, and the 40+-year-olds are most optimistic.

I wonder why this might be the case for these 3 countries. A generational change in world view? Is it politically, economically, or culturally based? The US and Ukraine have similar outlooks; however, they are very different counties. What might be common between these two countries that causes similar percentages?

This relates to my community and I through the idea that we are a data point on this graph. This graph can help us understand not only where we as a generation stand in terms out the future outlook, but where we as a country stand in respect to other countries. This may be able to shorten a generational gap, allowing us to put ourselves in our elders shoes and better understand their point of view.

This graph compares each countries percentage of 15-24 year olds who have an optimistic outlook on the future of our world, and the percentage of 40+ year olds who don't. A catchy title for this graph might be "The Generational Divide"

I notice the large division line separating the percentage of 15 to 24 year olds who say the world is getting better with each generation versus the percentage of 40+ year olds. What do you wonder?

Considering that they are using 1,000 people to represent countries filled with millions upon millions of people, the margin of error has to be pretty large. I also wonder how much the generational effect holds true. This graph would go to prove how people that have seen more have less optimism, but I wonder why there are so many 15-24 year olds that are hopeless for the future generations. 
How does this relate to you and your community?

If I were asked the same question, I would likely say that the world is not getting better with each generation because of certain things I have learned over the years. comments.raw_comment:
I notice that poor countries such as Nigeria, India, Ethiopia, and Bangladesh have a higher percentage of the population that thinks optimistically. On the contrary, more developed nations such as France and Spain have far higher levels of pessimism, especially amongst the older generations. group.  

I wonder why countries such as Japan have such high levels of pessimism amongst their older generations as opposed to their younger foes. I’m also very curious about why Indonesia is such an outlier in the graph. The country is not fully developed compared to its American and European counterparts.  Also, why does the graph omit 25 to 39-year-olds?

This graph relates to me and my community because we, Americans, are listed on the graph as the US. I’m part of the younger generation meaning that statistically, we are more optimistic than other first-world countries such as Germany, Japan, and Spain.

This graph is showing the levels of optimism amongst both younger and older generations. A younger audience is denoted by someone who is from 15 to 24 years old while the older audience is denoted by someone who is older than 40 years of age. The positive line of 1 shows equal thinking of both age groups. As a country gets further and further from the line, there is a larger disparity between the thinking of younger generations vs older ones. A catchy title would be “The surprising reality of optimism around the world.”

I also noticed that Indonesia has such a high percentage of people that think in both directions. It's important to know that younger people are more optimistic about future generations rather than the old people. I think that old people just think younger generations are annoying and unpatriotic, while younger people read history books and see how there were wars and bad things going on previously to their generation. I wonder why some countries are not very optimistic and some are. Is it the number of old people in a country, the economic stability, or is it something else? This relates to me and my community because being optimistic about our future generations is very important, and in the U.S. we are pretty optimistic mainly in the younger ages. A catchy title could be "Excited for the future, maybe not."

comments.raw_comment: This graph serves to compare adolescents (15-24) and adults (40+) and their level of optimism for the future of their country. I noticed in the graph that typically the younger generations had more optimism. This is because the majority of the 15-24 year old responses in the graph were above the line that was used to show how similar the younger and older adults' answers were for each country. For example, India's point is very close to the line, which therefore shows that India's adolescents and older adults have a very similar response. Along with this information, I also noticed that the countries with the highest optimism were countries that are still developing and are continuously growing and improving. I wonder why Brazil and Mali are so low on the graph. I also wonder what determines levels of optimism. I want to know why adults are generally less optimistic. Could this be because they have more life experience and have more realistic expectations? This relates to me and my community because I am in high school and I  live in the United States. I would say that the information in the graph accurately reflects my country. A good title for this graph could be: "Country Optimism Through the Ages"

comments.raw_comment:
This graph offers incite about how different generations view the future of the world. It asks 15-24 and 40+ year olds is the world is getting better with each generations. This graph depicts many more countries such as Brazil, Japan, the US and Zimbabwe showing 15-24 year olds saying the world gets better with each generation. On the opposing side, few countries such as Nigeria, India and Morocco have adults over the age of 40 agreeing the world gets better with each generation. Within theses graphs you can also see the percentage of people that are in agreement. Mali and Brazil, for example, both had a little more than 25% agree the world is getting better. I wonder why these countries are so low and why countries like Ethiopia and Zimbabwe are much more in favor of this question. Being in the 15-24 year old generation I think me and my friends have more faith in the younger generations than my parents generation, who still have more than my grandparents generation. It causes me wonder about if your lack of faith in the next generation lowers over time. 

Catchy Headline: "Generational Effect"

1. I noticed that out of all of the countries, there were only 3 countries whose adults over 40 years old believe that the world is getting better. But even then, only 45-60% of adults in these countries actually believe this. 

Indonesia is the only country where over 75% of its population of 15-24 year olds things the world is getting better. The rest of the countries' percentage of believers range from anywhere between 25%-75%. 

2. I wonder how human development influenced these results. Around 15-24 years of age, you slowly but surely start to lose your innocence as more terrible aspects of the world become clear. That may be why so few people in that age range actually believe that the world can experience a positive change. The older you get, however, you will witness so many changes since the years you were young, especially technological and medical advancements making life more convenient for others. 

The graph also shows that this works the other way. The greater abundance of countries whose 15yr-24yr population have high faith in the future may have to do with youthful thinking and hope before it gets shattered with more experience (most likely corresponding with more years of living). 

3. The age range of people in my town is a bit over 40 years, and this makes me intrigued to learn more about our ways of thinking and view on if future improvements are feasible. 

4. "Has Hope For Our Future Decreased? Here's 40 Countries' Input for Why and Why Not"

comments.raw_comment: What I find both interesting and predictable is that in most countries, there are more 15-24-year-olds than 40+-year-olds who think that the world is getting better with each generation. It took me a second to recognize, but the countries on the top left side of the line (positive residual) have higher percentages of younger adults than older adults who believe that the world is getting better, while on the bottom right (negative residual) show that the older adults think that the world is getting better more than, the younger adults. It makes sense that older people wouldn't believe that the world is improving since there are more progressive young adults and conservative older adults. This leads me to wonder, how would these statistics change as time continues to progress and younger adults become older adults? Since new concepts are built each generation, it makes sense that those older than the latest generation would have a hard time understanding how the world is changing and thus not want it to change. This is important to remember to ensure that the world truly continues to get better and that all generations can be excited and confident about those changes.

comments.raw_comment:
The most evident feature of this graph is that the amount of people aged 15-24 believe that the world gets better with each generation is very large, compared to the other portion of the graph, describing 40+ year olds. The second thing that I noticed was that the countries inside of the 40+ boundary are not in Europe or the Americas, but in Africa and Asia. Does that show that middle aged adults are more confident in their successors compared to the west? Another thing that I noticed is that the younger generations feel much better about themselves versus the older generations. The disconnect between young people and older people about the future is more alarming than anything else.

The biggest thing that I wonder is how the younger generation is so optimistic, given that many of their key development years have been distorted due to the pandemic. Adults have had the privilege to go through decades of their lives without worrying the virus, so naturally shouldn't they be more hopeful that things would go back to normal?

This affects me and my community because my life has been effected because of growing up in the pandemic. As a member of the 15-24 year old group, I can say that we've been able to find hope and happiness despite all of the negative things that have been happening in the world. I think it's important for the older generations to find some too.

In general, people who lives in Africa are more optimistic (India and Nigeria have a high percentage of optimism and a higher percentage from older generation than younger generation) because the shift in living condition and economic growth that the people have witnessed. The audience of the graph may be people from a wide range of countries and ages.

comments.raw_comment: This scatter plot, representing the data between two discrete variables with moderate positive correlation, shows how young adults (ages 15-24 years old) are more optimistic than 40+ years old adults. The audience can be psychologists, therapists, counselors, or anyone concerned about mental health, directing them towards pessimistic adults and offering help. The meaning of this plot can mean the world is becoming a better place because present young adults didn’t have to experience as much pain or suffering the 40+ years old adults did when they were younger. Another takeaway could be that older people have learned the negativity in our world through life experiences; hence, they are less optimistic. For instance, young adults could have big or unrealistic dreams and hopes for their future career, lifestyle, income, etc. But as they age, realizing the realities of how the real world works, it's easy to see why the older adults are less optimistic. The purpose of this plot is to compare and contrast how two different groups of people view our world, providing data for anyone interested.

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph relates the optimism between generations about the future for people from 21 countries.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

comments.raw_comment: The scatter graph shows the comparison of generation z(15-24) and generation x(40+), clearly with the younger generation of the sample being more optimistic towards improvement in the world. This graph would help us and geographers understand some people's views, which could lead to further research into why the younger generations have a positive prospect on their generation. It's indisputable that for even the most pessimistic country, Mali, the younger generation of the sample agrees that the world is improving. Why would the younger generations be so optimistic, why would the older generation be so pessimistic? There are many plausible reasons for this, firstly, the younger generation is born into a relatively more privileged and peaceful era, the worst a gen z could go through is the SARS or COVID-19 epidemics. I would say that most gen z's aren't hit by reality yet, the capacity for a gen z to think broad and critically is inferior to a gen x, the youth has baseless ambitions for future success, or rather, hasn't been hit by reality yet. Gen x is more pessimistic as they have most likely been hit with life and given up on some, they do not have the important resource - youth, health - that gen z has. This graph does show good news, improvement of any scale requires people with ambitions, and this graph ensures us that gen z's have the confidence of creating a better world.

comments.raw_comment:
I have noticed that this graph is a stacked scatter plot, which consists of participants from 7 African countries, 6 Asian countries, 4 American countries, and 4 European countries. The survey was fairly distributed (based on diversity) in these aspirations of generations bettering the world as time progresses. I have also noticed the lack of 40+ year-old participants, which I perceive as a sign that their opinion is rather less significant in this topic, because their generation has fundamentally passed. I believe that 15–24-year old’s are more reliable in this survey, because they are the current generation and could be considered as people who still have time to take new steps to better the world. The graph clearly shows a larger percentage of people aged 15-24 think the world is getting better. Third world countries have greater optimism with the world getting better hopefully meaning that these countries are receiving more support or are developing at a faster rate. The older you get the less optimistic you get about the world which shows that experiences have a lot to say about the way that you view the earth. The more experiences you have, the more negative your thoughts are which can show that the world isn't actually getting better and you could conclude that people aged 15-24 have less leverage due to their lack of experience and existence on the face of the earth. Younger generations have not seen the world change as much as older people which means that people aged 40+ are able to make a clearer judgement when it comes to the world getting better. However, there is no single generation that conclusively thinks the world is getting better which clearly shows that personal experiences (that do not relate to the world as a whole) have a massive effect on your judgement of the question. 

I wonder whether we can ever say that the world is getting better. Will there ever be a time when that statement is true?

Growing up as Gen Z, I have seen the personalities of other peers and I can say that Gen Z is a forward-thinking generation that is inclusive of all people. This can help the world be better to a certain extent.

What do you notice?
Like many others I noticed that young people seem a lot more hopeful in terms of the future however more specifically people in what I imagine to be "developing countries" everyone is a lot more hopeful than the general first world countries where adults don't seem as hopeful. 

What do you wonder?
As a child we have grown up in the age of technology meaning we are surrounded by the media. In my experience this means being surrounded with statements about the world dying due to climate change or a political debate or the earth splitting into millions of pieces. However I have never felt threatened by this so I wonder why young adults are not loosing hope about our future. How are we not more influenced by the media into losing hope for the future?

How does this relate to you and your community?
Although Australia isn't on the graph I still find myself relating to the data. I think some older people in the community are loosing hope and going further perhaps"giving up". They are not going of be around for all of our future therefore it is not as relevant.

For example, Napoleonic period for France and the Golden Age for the UK. comments.raw_comment:
Ignorance is Bliss?

 **What do you notice?**

I notice that in general, young people, aged 15-24 are more optimistic about the future than older people aged over 40. In developed countries of greater wealth, the divide between the youth and over 40s is more significant compared to the difference in less wealthy countries. Surprisingly, the quality of life in the countries doesn’t seem to have a clear relationship with the optimism of its people, with several countries that have a large percentage of its people in poverty or in conflict ranking higher than that of the USA, Germany, Japan and France. 

- **What do you wonder?**

I wonder why Indonesian youth adults are so positive about the future in comparison to other countries and whether this has to do with their quality of life, culture and government system. I also wonder what causes people, in general, to become less hopeful for the future when they are older, and whether the hopes of young people are misplaced and a result of naive idealism and the belief that they have the power to change the future for the better. Is it because older people have less faith in the younger generations that they believe that things will get worse?

* Why is Indonesia so optimistic? Is it because of their belief, or their schooling, or something else?
* How did they decide which countries to interview? Why wasn’t some countries on the graph, like Thailand or China?
* How come the young adults tend to be more optimistic than adults? Is it because the adults have been there to witness and contribute to the damage of the Earth? Or do the young adults have a more open mind set? Or something else?

A headline could be: Optimistic or Not About the Future?

comments.raw_comment: [4/5] I wonder if the poll is deemed adequately convincing since the 1,000 respondents on average from each country represent only a tiny portion of the countries’ total population. One thousand people out of the U.K.’s 67 million people is a mere 0.0015%, which cannot precisely tell what the people of the U.K. generally think about this question. In addition, these interviews are not done in person or through video chats, but through telephone calls, which means that respondents don't have to take it seriously. This further takes away the credibility of the polls. While we could argue that covering 1,000 respondents from every country is still a pretty large sample size since it’s not possible to cover everybody or interview everybody in person, we should still leave our doubts on the credibility of the polls. In addition, the poll was asking respondents to address what they think regarding the entire world, but most people might only think about their own country, because that’s what matters most to them and that’s what they care about, but what they think about their own countries do not necessarily have a relationship with whether or not the world is getting better. This potential loophole could also adulterate the authenticity and relevance of the survey results regarding the question. But despite all these accounts, this was still an interesting survey that is worthy of noting and further researching.

comments.raw_comment: [2/5] Overall, the number of global and regional crises did not fall but rather got bigger after the Cold War ended in 1991 when a new world order originally endowed with hope was established. Adults who are aged more than 40 have had enough of these havocs, and they have been hoping that things will gradually settle down when the U.S.S.R. collapsed. However, the exact opposite has happened. The disappointment is huge, and so did the hope of having a nonviolent world drop. This should happen to be the answer to why adults aged more than 40 are generally more pessimistic about the current world than young adults aged between 15 to 24 in the poll. These young adults grew up in the best of times with pervasive high-end technologies and democracies, so they have no idea what the quadragenerians have lived through in their childhood and adolescence, which was an era dominated by political animosity between Western democracies and Eastern communist dictatorships, giving rise to a myriad of global conflicts. That explains why younger adults have generally more positive thoughts on the world’s status quo.

comments.raw_comment: [3/5] The second thing I noticed is that there isn’t a clear cause-and-effect relationship between a country’s status quo and the percentage of people in that country who think the world is getting better. Let’s take Brazil and India, who have both been involved in unpleasant domestic situations for the past decade, where Brazil has been struggling to keep the Amazon Rainforest sustainable since the wildfire disaster occurred in 2019, and India has one of the worst covid-19 pandemic situations in the world as of 2021. While both Brazil and India seem to be going through a very rough time, there’s a surprisingly huge gap between the number of Brazilians in the poll who deems that the world has gone better and the number of Indians who deems that the world has gone better. For Brazil, less than 30% of young adults and less than 25% of adults expressed optimism about the world’s status quo, compared to poll takers from India, where more than 60% of young adults and adults expressed optimism about the world’s status quo. Not only India but also countries such as the U.S., Ukraine, and Lebanon have also undergone rough times in recent years, but have more than half of its respondents expressed positive views regarding the poll question. This is an interesting phenomenon that is worthy of further investigation.

comments.raw_comment:
What I notice:
It is apparent that in most of the countries, 15-to 24-year-olds people are more likely to satisfy with the progress of improving the world than 40+year-olds people. The countries located close to the black line like Indonesia, India, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Morocco, and Mali have relatively less difference in thoughts between generations. Overall, relatively fewer people in Brazil, and Mali are satisfied with the world, and have a hopeful view of the future, whereas people in Indonesia are more hopeful about the progress for the past few years no matter which generation they’re in. Also, the countries possessing a higher percentage of satisfaction regardless of generation are not fully developed countries. The developed countries that lead the world’s economy are mostly located in the middle part like the US, Germany, the UK.
 
What I wonder: 
I wonder about the specific structure or environment of a country that impacts people to build the view of the society. For example, I wonder how the society in the United States influences the younger generation to get a positive view of the world, whereas the older generation tends to view the future negatively though they’re living at the same time.

Relation to my community:
As the graph shows, the society that I spent most of my lives in had a more positive view of the world among the younger generation, rather than 40+.

 A catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea:
Is the world indeed getting better?

comments.raw_comment:
"The Opinions of Generations!"

First of all the most noticeable thing on the graph is that more 15-24-year-olds voted than 40+ year-olds. Another point to be made is within the 15-24-year-olds category there are many more countries and many of them are more developed compared to the countries in the 40+ year-olds category. This leaves me wondering why these countries have the response they do and why these questions were targeted specifically towards these generations. As a member of the 15-24-year-old category, I am exposed to many online sources for me to access information on the latest political and social news happening in all parts of the world. I feel as if this access to daily events gives me an advantage and a more open-minded opinion on this matter. 40+ year-olds come from a very different generation and have been raised differently and would most likely not have the knowledge or access to the internet as other generations who use it in their daily lives. Many 40+ year-olds do have the knowledge and are also exposed to the media but in a different way to how we use it. As to what is happening in the graph I believe a majority of 15-24-year-olds said that the world is getting better with each generation because we are the ones who will be living in it for a longer time and molding it into our own world. I trust the results of this graph even though I may disagree with them however, I support UNICEF so I am interested in discovering the reason behind these results.

comments.raw_comment:
1. It is apparent that in most of the countries, 15-to 24-year-olds people are more likely to satisfy with the progress of improving the world than 40+year-olds people. The countries located close to the black line like Indonesia, India, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Morocco, and Mali have relatively less difference in thoughts between generations. Overall, relatively fewer people in Brazil, and Mali are satisfied with the world, and have a hopeful view of the future, whereas people in Indonesia are more hopeful about the progress for the past few years no matter which generation they’re in. Also, the countries possessing a higher percentage of satisfaction regardless of generation are not fully developed countries. The developed countries that lead the world’s economy are mostly located in the middle part like the US, Germany, the UK.

2. I wonder about the specific structure or environment of a country that impacts people to build the view of the society. For example, I wonder how the society in the United States influences the younger generation to get a positive view of the world, whereas the older generation tends to view the future negatively though they’re living at the same time.

3. As the graph shows, the society that I spent most of my lives in had a more positive view of the world among the younger generation, rather than 40+.

4. Is the world indeed getting better?

comments.raw_comment:
Title: Boomers are a Downer!

This graph shows that, at a global level, young people are more optimistic about the world than older people.  There are a few places where - by a narrow margin - older people are more positive, but it is more common for young people to be substantially more optimistic.  Japan and the US stand out as having round about a 40% gap between proportions of young and old saying the world is getting better.  This is an interesting counterpoint to many discourses around generational attitudes: especially the notion that GenZ is somehow more 'cynical', and also the evidence that the younger generation has a much worse time than the baby boomers when it comes to job security and home ownership prospects.
